The bound error-rate series reflects this burstiness: median 0, mad 0, mean 313.8723404255319148936170212765957 errors/minute, max 1244, slope_per_second -0.01572617946345975948196114708603145, split_half_shift 0 (no trend).

Headline selection is UNAVAILABLE (selected false, reason GENUINE_PARTIAL_UNCALIBRATED) with all p-values null. The diagnostic summary reports anomalies_tested 0 and episodes_reported 0 with status COMPLETE and uncertainty NOT_ESTIMATED, so the three visible bursts were not machine-evaluated as episodes.

Timing/scope limits: resource_binding mode is run_intersection with clock_alignment "not_verified_by_core"; it drops 1 leading cell (dropped_leading_millis 4232) and 1 trailing cell (dropped_trailing_millis 10768); run window 1790628790768→1790629510768 (720000 ms), evaluation window 1790628795000→1790629500000 (705000 ms), snapshot window 1790628720000→1790629575000 (855000 ms). Window metrics use 73813 of the 75411 overall samples (1598 excluded), so overall and window figures differ slightly (p99 157 vs 158 ms). Because clock alignment is unverified, no lead/lag ordering between error bursts, resource changes and load phases is supportable from this evidence. hypotheses.observation: All 3688 errors in the overall scope (3688/75411) are reported under the single transaction label "checkout" (3688/12567, ~29.3%), while the other five labels — add product to cart (0/12569), cart (0/12568), home (0/12569), product (0/12569), reset cart (0/12569) — report zero errors. The policy FAIL comes from rule overall-errors on 3688/73813 versus lte 0.01.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: The failure may be specific to the checkout path (a checkout-only dependency, checkout request payload/validation, or a checkout-specific assertion) rather than a system-wide overload; the overall ~5% ratio may simply be the ~29% checkout failure rate diluted across six roughly equal transaction labels. This is a hypothesis, not an established cause.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Pull the failed checkout rows from the JTL (response code, response message, failure reason, thread group) and compare them with the frontend.request_error documents; confirm whether the 3688 OpenSearch errors and the 3688 failed checkout samples are the same events, and identify which downstream call each failure occurred on.

hypotheses.observation: In the error profile's own 15 s-step timeline, all errors fall in three bursts with starting cells at 1790628855000, 1790629095000 and 1790629335000 — exactly 240000 ms apart — and every other cell has count 0. Burst counts are 1363, 809 and 1516 (sum 3688) with peak rates 1232, 1224 and 1244 errors/minute. Separately, the run window in the resource binding spans 1790628790768→1790629510768, i.e. 720000 ms = 3 x 240000 ms.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: A recurring, roughly periodic driver may switch the checkout path into a failing state once per ~240 s cycle — candidates include a scheduled/periodic task, cache or credential expiry, connection-pool/lease recycling, a repeating load-generator phase, or periodic fault injection. The 720000 ms run length being exactly three 240 s cycles is suggestive but, because clock_alignment is "not_verified_by_core", the bursts cannot yet be placed within run cycles.
hypotheses.recommended_check: First verify clock alignment between the JMeter/core run clock, the metrics source and the OpenSearch error index. Then overlay the load-generator schedule (thread-group start/ramp/duration, any 240 s loops) and any cron/periodic job or TTL configuration on the three burst onsets and test whether a 240 s period explains them.

hypotheses.recommended_check: Inspect paymentservice restart count, container lifecycle/OOMKilled events and logs for the run period; list the epoch of each low-memory cell and each missing cell and check whether they co-occur; only after clock verification, compare those epochs with the three burst onsets.

hypotheses.observation: Checkout latency is p50 62 ms, p95 97 ms, p99 112 ms but max 10008 ms; the overall scope reports the same max of 10008 ms. With 12567 checkout samples, a p99 of 112 ms implies only on the order of 1% (~126 samples) exceed 112 ms.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: The 10008 ms value sits just above a round 10000 ms boundary and may reflect a client- or server-side timeout ceiling affecting a very small number of checkout samples, while the bulk of failures (if the failing samples are the fast ones) return quickly. Whether failures are fast errors or timeouts cannot be determined from these aggregates.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Split the checkout sample set into successful and failed rows and compare their elapsed-time distributions; check for a cluster at or just under 10008 ms; then compare the configured JMeter HTTP sampler connect/response timeout and the frontend/checkout HTTP client timeouts against 10000 ms.
